extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and politically engaged readers evaluating the proposed U.S. Constitution (late-18th-century ratification audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging whether a proposed constitution conforms to republican principles, whether it is federal or national in character, and whether a convention was authorized to propose such a constitution. Includes evaluation of the necessity and scope of powers conferred on a general government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a republic
rubrics_metrics.description: A republic is a government which derives all its powers directly or indirectly from the great body of the people, and is administered by persons holding their offices during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ESSENTIAL: that it be derived from the great body of the society, not from an inconsiderable proportion or a favored class; otherwise oligarchies might claim the name. SUFFICIENT: that persons administering it be appointed either directly or indirectly by the people and hold appointments by one of the tenures specified (during pleasure, for a limited period, or during good behavior). Examples: House elected immediately by the people; Senate appointed indirectly; judges holding by good behavior. Anti-pattern: derivation from a small, favored class claiming republican title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment modes and tenures as indicators of republican character
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how officers are appointed and the duration/tenure of their offices (immediate election, indirect appointment, fixed terms, good-behavior tenure) to determine conformity to republican standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare to State constitutions' models: House of Representatives elected immediately by the people; Senate derives appointment indirectly from the people (as in existing Congress); President indirectly derived from the choice of the people; judges hold by good behavior. Term-length comparisons (e.g., House 2 years, Senate 6 years, President 4 years) are used to show conformity to republican examples. Use these appointment and tenure features as evidence for or against a republican complexion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of titles of nobility and guaranty of republican form
rubrics_metrics.description: The absolute prohibition of titles of nobility (federal and state) and the express guaranty of a republican form of government to each State are decisive proofs of republican character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit constitutional prohibitions and guarantees (e.g., no titles of nobility; guarantee clause to states) as strong, nearly dispositive indicators that a system is republican in nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character by foundation: who ratifies (federal vs national foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To judge whether a government is federal or national, examine the foundation: whether the Constitution is founded on the assent and ratification of the people as one aggregate nation, or on the assent and ratification of the people as composing distinct and independent States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If assent/ratification is given by the people acting as constituent States (each State as a sovereign body), the act is federal; if it results from the majority of all individuals in the Union, it is national. Note: the method of ratification (state conventions vs aggregate popular vote) is critical to classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character by sources of ordinary powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the sources from which the ordinary powers of government are drawn: powers derived from the people (in national proportion) indicate national character; powers derived from the States as political societies indicate federal character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: House deriving powers from the people suggests national features; Senate deriving appointment from States on principle of equality suggests federal features. Evaluate each branch or power by its source to determine mixed or predominant character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character by operation of powers (on states vs individuals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish whether the government's powers operate on the political bodies composing the Confederacy (States, in their political capacities) or on individual citizens (in their individual capacities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If powers operate on States as collective political units (e.g., controversies where States are parties), this is federal; if powers operate directly on individuals (ordinary legislation, enforcement), this is national. Many powers may be national in ordinary operation even in a mixed system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character by extent of powers (indefinite supremacy vs enumerated/residuary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the government's jurisdiction is indefinite and supreme over persons/things (national), or whether jurisdiction is limited to enumerated objects with residuary sovereignty left to States (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A national government implies indefinite supremacy, able to control or abolish local authorities; a federal government has enumerated powers leaving residuary sovereignty to States. Use the scope and limitations of enumerated powers to judge extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character by amendment authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the mode by which future changes are introduced: whether ultimate authority to alter the government resides in a majority of the people (national) or in the concurrence of each State (federal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The required proportions and the unit of computation (states vs citizens) indicate leaning. Requiring more than a simple majority and computing proportions by States leans federal; allowing fewer than unanimous State concurrence leans national. The amendment procedure therefore helps locate the system on the federal–national spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate constitution as a composite (mixed) government across relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the Constitution separately in relation to its foundation, sources of powers, operation of powers, extent of powers, and amendment authority; the result may be a composition of federal and national features rather than wholly one or the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison's synthesis: foundation — federal; sources — partly federal partly national; operation — national; extent — federal; amendment — neither wholly. Use a multi-relational checklist to avoid crude binary labels and to identify where federal or national tendencies predominate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for construing the convention's authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the powers of a constitutional convention by inspecting the commissions given to its members and by construing recommendatory acts (e.g., Annapolis, Congress), allowing each part of the expression to have meaning and, when conflict exists, yielding the less important to the more important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two construction rules: (1) every part of the expression ought, if possible, to be allowed some meaning; (2) where parts cannot coincide, the less important should give way to the more important (means sacrificed to the end). Apply these rules to reconcile possibly conflicting mandates (e.g., ‘alterations in the Articles’ vs ‘provide a firm national government’).

rubrics_metrics.name: When exceeding formal commission may be justified by duty/necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether circumstances of crisis, public expectation, precedent, and the necessity of substantial reform could justify a convention's recommending measures beyond strict commissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors supporting extra-authority action include (a) a deep and unanimous impression of national crisis, (b) public expectation and demand for reform, (c) precedents of informal or assumed propositions justified by urgent occasions (e.g., Annapolis example), and (d) the submission of any proposed plan to the people themselves for final approval. The ultimate prudential test: accept advice based on whether the advice is good, not merely on its source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratification as federal act by State assent (not aggregate majority)
rubrics_metrics.description: View the establishment of the Constitution as the assent and ratification of the several States (each as a sovereign body) given by deputies elected for that purpose, not as the act of the people in one aggregate national capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because ratification is to result from the unanimous assent of the several States (expressed by their own people or conventions), the act is federal in foundation. This contrasts with a national act that would bind minorities by a majority of all citizens. Note also the practical concession discussed: the plan may be carried into effect by nine States, which raised objections but was pragmatically defended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess aggregate power by necessity and safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging whether the aggregate power vested in the general government is excessive, first ask whether each power is a necessary means to a necessary end; then, if necessary, devise safeguards against abuse and perversion of that power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Madison reduces powers to classes to guide evaluation: (1) security against foreign danger; (2) regulation of intercourse with foreign nations; (3) maintenance of harmony among States; (4) miscellaneous objects of general utility; (5) restraint of States from injurious acts; (6) provisions for giving due efficacy to all these powers. Use this classification to test necessity and to design checks (limitations, enumerations, restraints). Example: declaring war clearly necessary; raising armies/fleets is entailed by that; but question the necessity of indefinite powers (e.g., maintaining forces in peace). Balance benefits against inevitable risks of abuse.
